title: What makes news worthy?
summary: This World News Day, Rappler celebrates what makes news worth reading, remembering, and supporting — and opens the Rappler+ community to more people with a special annual rate of P2,800 from…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Every day, newsrooms decide what is newsworthy. What affects our lives? Who should be held accountable? Which stories might change how we see our communities, or what we do next? Visit a news website, or scroll through a newsroom’s app, and you see the result of thousands of those decisions.
But this World News Day, we want to turn the question around: What makes news worthy?
Worthy of your attention. Worthy of acting on. And, increasingly, worthy of support.

We have never had easier access to information. An answer, post, or video is almost always a tap away. But more information has not necessarily made us better informed. Much of what reaches us now passes through platforms designed to maximize engagement. Algorithms increasingly influence what gets amplified, often rewarding the content most likely to keep us watching and doomscrolling.

Journalism works differently. Behind every investigation, fact-check, breaking story, and explainer are journalists doing the less visible work: finding sources, examining documents, going into communities, and asking difficult questions. That work requires people, expertise, and resources. Yet we have grown accustomed to receiving much of it for free. Across the world, the economic foundations of public-interest journalism have become increasingly fragile even as the need for credible information grows.
So perhaps the question isn’t simply: Why should I pay for news? It’s also: If everyone expects journalism to be free, who pays for the journalism society depends on?
This World News Day, Rappler is highlighting two initiatives that demonstrate what makes journalism worth sustaining – not only in the stories we publish, but in what those stories make possible.
A newsroom does more than publish information.

In the pursuit of stories, journalists encounter communities across nearly every part of society: students, teachers, workers, business leaders, activists, public servants, artists, experts, and ordinary citizens living through extraordinary events. News gives those communities something to gather around: a shared fact, a problem to solve, a question to pursue.

This September, MovePH’s Civic Circles brought different sectors together to talk about keeping schools safe following tragic incidents of violence in Philippine schools. The goal wasn’t simply to report the problem, but to create space for people to understand it together and ask: What can we do next?
That same belief in the power of information to create community is behind something else.
Rappler launched this September: MUNI.

Found at the heart of the word COMMUNITY and inspired by the Filipino muni-muni (to reflect), MUNI is a growing network of people, newsrooms, organizations, and communities built around trustworthy information, human accountability, and real connection. There is no algorithm deciding which conversation deserves your attention. The people and communities in the network do. Because information shouldn’t only tell us what’s happening. At its best, it should help us understand one another, and give us something to do together.
Know more about MUNI here.
But journalism has another kind of value — one that often becomes clearer with time. A headline might disappear from the homepage tomorrow. The events it documents don’t.

Before Rappler, there was Newsbreak. Founded in 2001, the award-winning news magazine became known for investigations and deeply reported stories that took readers behind the scenes of Philippine politics and power. Members of its team would later help build Rappler.

Now, Rappler is opening the Newsbreak Archives to Rappler+ annual members. Stories written years or decades ago can suddenly help explain a controversy unfolding today. An investigation becomes evidence. A profile becomes a record of power. Reporting from one political era becomes context for understanding the next. Before it was history, it was news.
The Newsbreak Archives remind us that news doesn’t expire simply because the news cycle moves on.
This World News Day, we are asking you to help sustain what makes all of this possible.

From September 23 to 28, Rappler+ annual membership is available at a special rate of P2,800 for one year. Your membership gives you access to Rappler+ journalism and experiences, including the Newsbreak Archives, while helping support the independent newsroom behind them.
So this World News Day, perhaps the question isn’t only about what is newsworthy.
Ask something bigger: What makes news worthy?

News is worthy when it helps us understand what matters. When it brings people together around facts instead of outrage. When today’s reporting becomes tomorrow’s historical record. And when it gives communities the information they need to decide what happens next.
